title: Superposition and Interference
lead: Most waves look complicated because they are several simple waves added together, and the rule for adding them is that the disturbances add. This section follows that rule to its ends: two identical waves in phase, which double; two exactly out of phase, which cancel; two running the opposite way, which stand still and give a string its fundamental and its overtones; and two of almost the same frequency, which beat.
objectives: Describe the mathematical representation of overtones and beat frequency.
summary_html:
• Superposition is the combination of two waves at the same location.
  • Constructive interference occurs when two identical waves are superimposed in phase.
  • Destructive interference occurs when two identical waves are superimposed exactly out of phase.
  • A standing wave is one in which two waves superimpose to produce a wave that varies in amplitude but does not propagate.
  • Nodes are points of no motion in standing waves.
  • An antinode is the location of maximum amplitude of a standing wave.
  • Waves on a string are resonant standing waves with a fundamental frequency and can occur at higher multiples of the fundamental, called overtones or harmonics.
  • Beats occur when waves of similar frequencies $\kfone$ and $\kftwo$ are superimposed. The resulting amplitude oscillates with a beat frequency given by $$\kfB = \lvert\kfone - \kftwo\rvert.$$

figures.original_caption: (Figure 16.33) Pure constructive interference of two identical waves produces one with twice the amplitude, but the same wavelength. (Figure 16.34) Pure destructive interference of two identical waves produces zero amplitude, or complete cancellation. (Figure 16.35) Superposition of non-identical waves exhibits both constructive and destructive interference.

Standing wave created by the superposition of two identical waves moving in opposite directions. The oscillations are at fixed locations in space and result from alternately constructive and destructive interference.
(Figure 16.37) The figure shows a string oscillating at its fundamental frequency. (Figure 16.38) First and second overtones are shown.

Beats are produced by the superposition of two waves of slightly different frequencies but identical amplitudes. The waves alternate in time between constructive interference and destructive interference, giving the resulting wave a time-varying amplitude.

exercises.prompt: Imagine you are holding one end of a jump rope, and your friend holds the other. If your friend holds her end still, you can move your end up and down, creating a transverse wave. If your friend then begins to move her end up and down, generating a wave in the opposite direction, what resultant wave forms would you expect to see in the jump rope?

answer.solution: The rope would alternate between having waves with amplitudes two times the original amplitude and reaching equilibrium with no amplitude at all. The wavelengths will result in both constructive and destructive interference
Nodes are areas of wave interference where there is no motion. Antinodes are areas of wave interference where the motion is at its maximum point.

exercises.prompt: You hook up a stereo system. When you test the system, you notice that in one corner of the room, the sounds seem dull. In another area, the sounds seem excessively loud. Describe how the sound moving about the room could result in these effects.

answer.solution: With multiple speakers putting out sounds into the room, and these sounds bouncing off walls, there is bound to be some wave interference. In the dull areas, the interference is probably mostly destructive. In the louder areas, the interference is probably mostly constructive.

exercises.prompt:
A guitar string has a number of frequencies at which it vibrates naturally. Which of the following is true in this context?
(a) The resonant frequencies of the string are integer multiples of fundamental frequencies.
(b) The resonant frequencies of the string are not integer multiples of fundamental frequencies.
(c) They have harmonic overtones.
(d) None of the above

answer.solution: The book gives no answer to this item, so work it out from the harmonics of a string fixed at both ends. The longest wavelength the string can carry is $\klamone = 2L$, so the lowest frequency is $\kfone = \kvw/2L$; the shorter standing waves that fit between the same two fixed ends have $\klamtwo = L$ and $\lambda_3 = 2L/3$, which give $\kftwo = 2\kfone$ and $\kfthree = 3\kfone$. The natural frequencies are therefore whole-number multiples of the fundamental, and those multiples are what the section calls the overtones or harmonics. Both (a) and (c) say something true of the string, and the reader who is asked for one answer should say why: (a) states the rule, and (c) names it.

exercises.prompt: Explain the principle of superposition with figures that show the changes in the wave amplitude.

answer.solution: The student explains the principle of superposition and then shows two waves adding up to form a bigger wave when a crest adds with a crest and a trough with another trough. Also the student shows a wave getting cancelled out when a crest meets a trough and vice versa.

figure.alt: Two wave generators are shown with their resulting rarefaction and compression marked. Points A, C, D, and E are at the intersection of two compression lines. Point B is at the intersection of two rarefaction lines. Point F is at the intersection of a compression line and a rarefaction line.
figure.caption: Two wave generators send out compressions and rarefactions that cross at the points A to F.

exercises.prompt:
In this figure which points represent the points of constructive interference?
(a) A, B, F
(b) A, B, C, D, E, F
(c) A, C, D, E
(d) A, B, D

answer.solution: The book gives no answer to this item, so read it off the figure. Constructive interference happens where the two generators send the same kind of disturbance to the same place, so that the disturbances add: a compression meeting a compression, or a rarefaction meeting a rarefaction. Points A, C, D and E are each where two compression lines cross, and B is where two rarefaction lines cross, so all five add constructively. Point F, where a compression meets a rarefaction, is the one place the disturbances are in opposite directions and subtract, which is destructive interference.

exercises.prompt: A string is fixed on both sides. It is snapped from both ends at the same time by applying an equal force. What happens to the shape of the waves generated in the string? Also, will you observe an overlap of waves?

answer.solution: The student must note that the shape of the wave remains the same and there is first an overlap and then receding of the waves.

exercises.prompt: In the preceding question, what would happen to the amplitude of the waves generated in this way? Also, consider another scenario where the string is snapped up from one end and down from the other end. What will happen in this situation?

answer.solution: The book gives no answer to this item, so work it from the rule that the disturbances add. Two pulses snapped upward with equal force are identical waves arriving in phase, so where they meet their amplitudes add and the string rises to twice the amplitude of either pulse; that is pure constructive interference, and once the pulses have passed through each other each carries on with its own amplitude again. Snapped up at one end and down at the other, the two pulses are equal and opposite, so where they meet the disturbances are in opposite directions and cancel: the string is momentarily flat, which is pure destructive interference, and again the two pulses emerge unchanged and travel on.

exercises.prompt: Two sine waves travel in the same direction in a medium. The amplitude of each wave is $A$, and the phase difference between the two is 180°. What is the resultant amplitude?

answer.hint: A phase difference of 180° puts every crest of one wave on a trough of the other.

exercises.prompt: Standing wave patterns consist of nodes and antinodes formed by repeated interference between two waves of the same frequency traveling in opposite directions. What are nodes and antinodes and how are they produced?

answer.solution: The book gives no answer to this item, so answer it from the section’s definitions. Nodes are the points where the string does not move, and more generally they are the places where the wave disturbance is zero in a standing wave; an antinode is the place where the amplitude of the standing wave is greatest. They are produced by the two waves running in opposite directions through each other: at a node the two disturbances are always equal and opposite, so they cancel at every moment, while at an antinode they are always equal and in the same direction, so they add and the point swings through twice the amplitude of either wave. A node and an antinode are a quarter of a wavelength apart, and the fixed ends of a string must be nodes because the string cannot move there.

exercises.prompt: Speakers in stereo systems have two color-coded terminals to indicate how to hook up the wires. If the wires are reversed, the speaker moves in a direction opposite that of a properly connected speaker. Explain why it is important to have both speakers connected the same way.

answer.solution: A speaker cone pushes the air in front of it outward to make a compression and draws back to make a rarefaction, and the terminals decide which way it moves for a given signal. When both speakers are connected the same way they move together, so the two sound waves arrive at the listener in phase and their disturbances add: the low notes, whose wavelengths are long enough that the two speakers are close together compared with a wavelength, interfere constructively and sound full. Reverse the wires on one speaker and it moves out while the other moves in, so the two waves arrive exactly out of phase, crest against trough, and interfere destructively. The bass, which the two speakers reproduce alike, then largely cancels and the sound goes thin.

exercises.prompt: A car has two horns, one emitting a frequency of 199 Hz and the other emitting a frequency of 203 Hz. What beat frequency do they produce?

answer.hint: The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies.

exercises.prompt: Two tuning forks having frequencies of 460 and 464 Hz are struck simultaneously. What average frequency will you hear, and what will the beat frequency be?

parts.hint: The resultant runs at the average of the two frequencies.
The amplitude fluctuates at the difference of the two frequencies.

exercises.prompt: A wave traveling on a Slinky® that is stretched to 4 m takes 2.4 s to travel the length of the Slinky and back again. (a) What is the speed of the wave? (b) Using the same Slinky stretched to the same length, a standing wave is created which consists of three antinodes and four nodes. At what frequency must the Slinky be oscillating?

parts.hint: The wave covers the length twice in that time.

parts.part: (b) the frequency of the standing wave
parts.hint: Three antinodes and four nodes are three loops, so the wavelength is two thirds of the length.
